title: Geoffrey Garrett - Podcast - In Good Company - Norges Bank Investment Management

meta.source: Macro Transcripts/Geoffrey Garrett - Podcast - In Good Company - Norges Bank Investment Management.docx

speakers: Geoffrey Garrett (Dean, USC Marshall School of Business)
Nicolai Tangen (CEO, Norges Bank Investment Management)
summary: May 2025 NBIM podcast, mostly about leadership and business education; the only macro-relevant content is Garrett view that shrinking global markets and reshoring raise prices and interest rates, Chinese EVs as a transformative force, Norway EV adoption by policy design, and AI job disruption.

coverage.note: nothing actionable: leadership skills and teaching
nothing actionable: admissions, COVID leadership lessons
nothing actionable: curriculum and talent search
AI job disruption view; ROI of degrees otherwise nothing actionable
nothing actionable: CEO traits, delegation, time
nothing actionable: leadership style in academia
nothing actionable: academia-business ties, research funding
shrinking global markets; otherwise MBA education
reshoring costs, Kantian trade-peace, Norway EVs, Chinese EVs
German autos and China, EV labor, green supply chain, career optionality

completeness_estimate: 0.95 - interview is mostly leadership and business-education talk with no macro content; first reader caught nearly all the trade, EV and AI points, missing only the ICE phase-out remark; one speaker mix-up.

claims.speaker: Geoffrey Garrett
claims.quote: there's a lot of job disruption and displacement in the short term but
claims.claim: AI may follow prior technological revolutions, with short-term job disruption and displacement followed by new job creation in the longer term.

claims.speaker: Geoffrey Garrett
claims.quote: the shrinking of global markets is going to is a big net negative
claims.claim: As a classic liberal economist, Garrett views the shrinking of global markets (more transactional, competing countries) as a major economic net negative.
claims.testable: partly - trade volume vs growth studies

claims.speaker: Geoffrey Garrett
claims.quote: globalization reduced prices and reduced interest rates in America for decades
claims.claim: Reshoring and tariffs carry a real cost in higher prices, and since globalization lowered prices and interest rates for decades, reversing it pushes both up.
claims.indicator: US consumer prices and interest rates vs trade openness
claims.direction: higher prices and rates from reshoring

claims.speaker: Geoffrey Garrett
claims.quote: if they if they can join activities, they're less likely to go to war against each other
claims.claim: Following Kant, closer economic ties lower the probability of war between countries, so decoupling raises geopolitical risk.

claims.speaker: Nicolai Tangen
claims.quote: I think the number now is something like 90% of new cars sold are electrical
claims.claim: Norway reached about 90% EV share of new car sales through large subsidies, a charging network, taxi-lane access and no annual fees, so policy design rather than cold weather determined adoption; US cheap petrol makes the same logic harder.
claims.indicator: EV share of new car sales
claims.conditions: subsidies plus infrastructure; relative fuel prices
claims.testable: yes - country EV share vs incentives

correction.issue: Mixed speakers: Tangen explains Norway's subsidies, charging network, taxi-lane access and no annual fees; the point that the US is a fossil-fuel exporter with the world's cheapest petrol, making EVs harder there, is Garrett's.
correction.fix: Nicolai Tangen: Norway reached about 90% EV share of new car sales through large subsidies, a nationwide charging network, taxi-lane access and no annual fees, so buying a combustion car made no economic sense. Garrett adds that cheap petrol in the US (a fossil-fuel exporter) makes the same logic harder there.

claims.speaker: Geoffrey Garrett
claims.quote: that's a transformative force for the global economy
claims.claim: The rise of Chinese EV makers (BYD, Xiaomi) is a transformative force for the global economy, and Europe and the US must decide whether to protect domestic automakers with tariffs.

claims.speaker: Geoffrey Garrett
claims.quote: if they protect it against Chinese electric vehicles, the Chinese, they're not going to have access to the Chinese market
claims.claim: Germany faces a trade-off: protecting its auto industry against Chinese EVs risks retaliation that closes the Chinese market it needs, with VW considering plant closures.
claims.direction: German auto exposure to China retaliation

claims.speaker: Geoffrey Garrett
claims.quote: You just need many, many fewer workers to put together an EV than a traditional combustion engine.
claims.claim: EVs are simpler to assemble, so a shift to EVs cuts manufacturing and auto employment, which affects political reactions in Europe and the US.

claims.speaker: Geoffrey Garrett
claims.quote: the entire green energy supply chain now is dominated by China
claims.claim: China dominates the green energy supply chain, which is power-intensive and dirty, and metals such as Indonesian nickel are needed for long-range EVs.

claims.speaker: Geoffrey Garrett
claims.quote: if we then in a like a two decade period do away with uh internal combustion engines, that'd be pretty amazing.
claims.claim: Garrett sees a possible phase-out of the internal combustion engine, the defining technology of the 20th century, within about two decades, a structural shift for autos, oil demand and metals supply chains.
claims.indicator: EV share of new car sales
claims.direction: ICE and oil demand down; battery metals demand up
claims.conditions: EV adoption continues at policy-driven pace
